description: One compliance rule, defined as DATA rather than as code: what it scans, what state makes it ripe, which regulation it answers to, and what it says when it fires. A RULE IS A RECORD ANYBODY CAN EDIT — a threshold moves, a citation is renumbered, an operator turns one off for a season, and none of it is a code release. WHAT DOES NOT MOVE IS THE ENGINE: evaluation is deterministic, reads the current state of the target records, and involves no model at sweep time. AI belongs at authoring time, behind a human approval, which is what `authored_by`, `ai_source_citation`, `human_approved_by` and `human_approved_on` are for — an auditor asking 'who decided this and when' reads the answer off the row. RULES ARE VERSIONED BY COPY, exactly as Inspection Templates are: an edit writes a NEW row at version+1 and points the old row's `superseded_by` at it, so a sweep already running against v1 sees a definition that cannot change underneath it, and an alert raised last April can still be read against the rule that raised it.

fields.description: The series a Compliance Rule is named from, expanded by the controller rather than by Frappe's naming_series hook so a docname is the same shape on a bench and in the standalone suite — CRULE-2026-0001. The year is the year the rule was authored, which is also the year an auditor asking 'when did you start looking for this' is after.
fields.label: Series

fields.description: The stable key this rule's alerts are filed under — `certification_expiring`, `training_expiring`. IT IS THE FIRST SEGMENT OF EVERY ALERT DOCNAME (`<rule_id>:<source_doctype>:<source_name>`), so it must never change on a live rule: changing it orphans every alert already raised, together with every snooze and every human dismissal somebody set on them. DELIBERATELY NOT UNIQUE AT THE SCHEMA LEVEL, because a rule is versioned by copy and v1 and v2 share a rule_id by construction. What may not exist twice is an ENABLED, unsuperseded row — enforced in the controller, and reflected on `active_row_flag`.
fields.label: Rule ID

fields.description: What the rule says, in the words somebody reads on a phone at seven in the morning — 'A certificate or licence is inside its renewal window', not 'rule 1'.
fields.label: Title

fields.description: Which shelf of the compliance calendar this rule's alerts land on. The calendar groups by it, and a category nobody uses is a group nobody opens. `Finance` arrived in v0.39.0 with the Financial KPI Framework, and it is on this list rather than on a second board because an operation with two alerting systems reads neither: a covenant about to be breached is exactly as much a Monday-morning problem as a cabin with a dead carbon monoxide detector, and both want the same dismissal, the same snooze and the same auto-clear when the condition stops being true.
fields.label: Category
fields.options:
Audits
Certifications
Filings
Finance
Housing
Inventory
Policies
Records
Spray and Pesticides
Water and Sanitation
Work Timing
Workforce

fields.description: Whether the sweep runs this rule. OFF IS NOT DELETED: an inactive rule raises nothing AND DISMISSES NOTHING, so the alerts it already owns stay exactly as they were — the same reading a rule skipped for a missing DocType gets, and for the same reason. A rule cannot be enabled until `human_approved_by` and `human_approved_on` are filled in; a new rule is therefore authored in Draft and approved before it can ever fire.
fields.label: Enabled

fields.description: THE TRANSACTION-TIME GATE THIS RULE GOVERNS, and the field that makes this row a GATE rather than a SWEEP. Blank on every rule authored before v0.80.0 and on every rule that watches the site on a cadence: those are scanned nightly, raise an alert about a record that has drifted, and dismiss it when the drift resolves. A rule with a control point is not scanned at all — it is consulted at the moment somebody tries to do the thing, by name, from the tool that does it. `approval_threshold` is asked before a spend is booked; `period_close_lockdown` before a posting lands in a closed month. WHY THE TWO KINDS SHARE ONE DOCTYPE. Because an operator asking 'what does this system check, and how hard' should get ONE register back, not two — and because everything that makes a swept rule auditable (the citation, the version-by-copy, the human approval, the purpose) is exactly what makes a gate auditable. What differs is when it runs, which is one field. `erpnext_mcp/enforcement.py` holds the list of control points that mean anything; a rule naming one this app does not implement is refused on save, because a control nothing consults is a control an operator believes they have.
fields.label: Control Point

fields.description: HOW HARD THIS GATE PUSHES, and the whole of what an operator turns up as they grow. ADVISORY (the default, and the default is the load-bearing part) means the control still runs, still decides, and still writes the finding to the compliance calendar as an alert against the record — and then LETS THE WORK THROUGH. ENFORCED means the same code reaches the same finding and refuses the action, naming what was wrong and what would make it right. THE CODE PATH AND THE DATA TRAIL ARE IDENTICAL EITHER WAY. That is the design: an operation runs a season in Advisory, reads the alerts the controls would have blocked on, fixes the ones that are real, widens the thresholds that are not, and turns the toggle over having already seen what it will cost. A control whose enforced behaviour is discovered on the day it is switched on is a control that gets switched off that afternoon. IT SHIPS ADVISORY FOR EVERY SEEDED CONTROL, deliberately. A four-person farm that cannot book a fuel invoice because nobody has been named an approver does not conclude that its controls need configuring; it concludes that this app is in the way.
fields.label: Enforcement

fields.description: Which version of this rule this row is. An edit through update_compliance_rule writes v+1 as a NEW row and never touches this one, so a sweep already walking v1 finishes against the definition it started with.
fields.label: Version

fields.description: The row that replaced this one. A soft supersede: this row is disabled, never deleted, so the definition an alert was raised under is still on the site in full.
fields.label: Superseded By

fields.description: Computed, never typed: 1 when this row is the one the sweep will run for its rule_id — enabled and not superseded. It is the column the 'one live row per rule_id' constraint is read off, and the one an index can answer 'what is the rule set tonight' from without joining.
fields.label: Active Row

fields.description: The DocType whose rows this rule walks. Required for a declarative rule; a rule that delegates to a shipped scanner or to custom_python still names it, because it is what an operator reads to know what the rule is about and what `requires_doctypes` defaults to.
fields.label: Target DocType

fields.description: Comma-separated DocTypes that must exist on the site for this rule to run at all. Defaults to `target_doctype`. A rule whose DocTypes are absent is SKIPPED, and skipping raises nothing and dismisses nothing — an absent DocType is not evidence that anybody did the work.
fields.label: Requires DocTypes

fields.description: Comma-separated fields that must exist on `target_doctype` for this rule to run — `i9_status`, `flc_license_expiration`. A compliance field this app installs on demand is absent on a site that has not run install_compliance_fields, and a rule that scanned for it anyway would report every employee as clean. The rule is skipped by name instead, which says what the fix is.
fields.label: Requires Fields

fields.description: The name of a scanner that SHIPS WITH THIS APP, for a rule whose gate is a shape no set of declarative fields expresses. Since v0.22.1 that is TWO rules and both are permanent: a child table walked and folded to its worst row, which is an aggregation rather than a filter; and a walk over a TABLE of doctypes whose thresholds mean days elapsed rather than days remaining. Everything else the v0.22.0 notes listed here — supersession by a later clean record, two dates that only matter together, several anchors of the same kind — is now a field. The record still owns everything an operator would change: the thresholds, the scope, the citations, the regimes, the message where the scanner uses one, and the switch. Only the SHAPE of the scan is code, and it is code that was reviewed, tested and shipped rather than typed into a text field. list_compliance_rules names the scanners this site has.
fields.label: Built-in Scanner

fields.description: THE ESCAPE HATCH, AND IT IS MEANT TO STAY SMALL. A short restricted-Python program, evaluated by this app's own AST interpreter — never `exec`, never `eval` — which is handed `frappe` (read-only helpers), `today`, the rule's thresholds and a small standard library, and returns a list of observations. `import`, `open`, `exec`, `eval`, `while`, `def`, `class`, `lambda` and every dunder attribute are refused, the step count is bounded and the wall clock is bounded. Prefer the declarative fields: every rule that needs this is a primitive this framework has not grown yet, and an AI-proposed rule with this field filled in is flagged for extra review precisely because a text field that runs is the one part of a data-defined rule that is not merely data.
fields.label: Custom Python

fields.description: A JSON list of ADDITIONAL doctypes this one rule walks, where a rule is genuinely about more than one kind of record — `[{"doctype": "Detector Test", "date_field": "test_date", "label": "the detector test"}]`. `target_doctype` above is the first and is singular by design; this is the exception, and it is a small one. A cabin with a water stain and a cabin with a dead CO detector are the same conversation with the same person on the same walk round the camp, and splitting them into two rule_ids would split one afternoon's work across two alert types — and change every alert docname on every site. `label` is the fragment the message says instead of the doctype name. A doctype in this list that a site has not got is skipped, not fatal.
fields.label: Additional Target DocTypes (JSON)

fields.description: The field on `target_doctype` the clock runs from — `expiration_date`, `last_habitability_inspection`, `review_due_date`. LEAVE IT EMPTY FOR A RULE WITH NO CLOCK: a rule whose whole condition is a scope filter (an I-9 recorded as Expired) fires on every matching row at `severity_expired`, which is the honest reading — the row is already past due by the only measure the rule has.
fields.label: Date Field

fields.description: Clock: the date is a DEADLINE and how far away it is decides the band. Timestamp: the date is WHEN THE THING WAS FOUND — read for the message, bands nothing, every matching row raises at Once Past Due. State (v0.22.5): the rule fires on a DATA STATE and not on any distance from a date — the gates decide, the date is read for the message only, and the severity is State-driven Severity.
fields.label: Date Field Role

fields.description: SEVERAL anchors of the same kind, where EITHER being stale fires the rule and the message must name which — `[{"field": "smoke_detector_last_test", "label": "smoke"}, {"field": "co_detector_last_test", "label": "CO"}]`. Each is measured against the same `cadence_days`; the severity is folded to the worst of them; the message gets `stale_dates` (one entry per field that is actually stale, with its label, its date and its age) and `first_stale_label`. 'The CO detector was last tested 400 days ago' is a different errand from 'no smoke detector test has ever been recorded', and an alert saying only 'a detector is overdue' sends somebody to test the wrong one. Overrides `date_field` when set.
fields.label: Date Fields (JSON)

fields.description: How often the activity must recur, in days. The due date is `date_field + cadence_days`, so 365 on a last-inspection date means the annual walk and 0 means the date field IS the deadline (an expiry, a review date). It is the real interval the thing takes in the world, not a reminder preference.
fields.label: Cadence (days)

fields.description: A field on the row carrying ITS OWN lead time in days, used in place of `threshold_warning_days` where it is set — `renewal_window_days` on a certificate, because the turnaround an issuing body actually takes is a property of the certificate and not of the rule. Empty means every row uses the rule's threshold.
fields.label: Per-row Window Field

fields.description: What a row with NO date in `date_field` means. `Skip` is right for an expiry — a training with no expiry does not lapse, and a renewal alert nobody can clear is how a calendar stops being read. `Raise` is right for a cadence — a cabin nobody has ever inspected is the most overdue cabin there is, and answering 'no date, no alert' would hide exactly the unit somebody needs to walk.
fields.label: When the date is missing

fields.description: What due date the alert carries. `From Anchor` is `date_field + cadence_days`, and is blank where the row has no date. `Today` is for a rule with no clock, whose condition is true now. `None` leaves it empty. The calendar sorts on it, so a rule that set the wrong one sorts wrongly rather than failing.
fields.label: Due Date

fields.description: A SECOND date, used only as a gate: the rule considers a row only where this date is inside `gate_within_days`. It is a conjunction over two independent dates, which the one cadence anchor above cannot express — a block raises a water-test alert when it was sprayed inside the season AND its water was tested outside the cadence, and neither half fires alone. Ground nobody is spraying raises nothing however stale its water. A row whose gate date is EMPTY is gated OUT: the gate is a claim that the condition matters now, and no date is no claim.
fields.label: Gate Date Field

fields.description: How recent `gate_date_field` must be for the row to be considered. 120 on a last-spray date is about one spray season in tree fruit: a block sprayed inside it will be sprayed again, and its water matters now.
fields.label: Gate Within (days)

fields.description: Where the gate date is read from. `Direct` is a column on the row being scanned. `Latest Related` is the newest date on another doctype pointing back at it, described in `gate_related_table_json` — which is what 'when was this block last sprayed' looks like on a site keeping a spray log rather than a column.
fields.label: Gate Scope

fields.description: For a `Latest Related` gate: `{"doctype": "Farm Task", "subject_field": "field", "date_field": "completed_on", "scope_filters": [...]}`. The newest `date_field` on a row of `doctype` whose `subject_field` names the row being scanned. Read ONCE PER SWEEP and folded to a per-subject maximum, not once per candidate — a camp with fifty cabins and four years of history is one query, not four hundred.
fields.label: Gate Related Table (JSON)
Latest Child Row Threshold (JSON)
fields.description: v0.22.5. The newest child row of each scanned record, and a number read off it. {"child_doctype", "parent_field", "order_by", "context_key", "match", "conditions": [{"field", "op", "threshold", "threshold_source"}], "scope_filters"}. A subject with no child row is gated OUT: a shift with an empty weather timeline is not a cool shift, it is a shift nobody has a reading for.

fields.label: Condition Tree (JSON)
fields.description: v0.233.0. The CCF generic evaluator (docs/design/ccf_core_work_timing.md §2). all / any / not nodes over leaves {path, op, value | value_source, agg?, id, reason {en, es}, basis, source}. Set, it replaces the primitive scan for this rule; blank, the rule runs as before. get_compliance_field_map lists every path under `context`.

fields.label: Evaluation (JSON)
fields.description: v0.233.0. {raise_when: fail (default — a Hold) | pass, as_of: today | tomorrow, when: [sweep, day_start, task_start, evening_cutoff, forecast_refresh], for_each}.

fields.label: Actions (JSON)
fields.description: v0.233.0. [{type: alert | create_farm_task | add_to_audit_packet | set_go_hold | block_start | require_override_reason | require_checklist_item | notify_workers | notify_supervisor | shift_dates, …}]. An alert is always raised; the others run as each feature lands.

Fire at `severity_critical` when this many days or fewer remain. NEGATIVE MEANS THE BAND NEVER FIRES — a rule that only has anything to say once the date has passed sets -1 here, and the row is then reached only by `severity_expired`. Whatever number is here should be the real lead time past which starting late means missing it, and somebody should be able to say where it came from.
fields.label: Critical Within (days)

fields.description: Fire at `severity_warning` when this many days or fewer remain and the critical band was not reached. It is also the window OUTSIDE which the rule says nothing at all: a certificate 200 days out raises nothing however often the sweep runs. Negative means the band never fires. Overridden per row by `window_field` where that is set.
fields.label: Warning Within (days)

fields.description: The severity of the critical band. Critical means something is blocked TODAY — a person cannot lawfully work, a block cannot lawfully be entered. A rule that raises Critical for something merely needing attention devalues the word for the rules that meant it.
fields.label: Critical Band Severity

fields.description: The severity of the warning band. Warning means it needs doing this month; Info is context, and is the right answer for a deadline that has not yet passed on something nobody is blocked by.
fields.label: Warning Band Severity

fields.description: The severity once the due date has PASSED — and, for a rule with no `date_field`, the severity every matching row raises. Separate from the bands because the two are different facts: a licence expiring in a fortnight and a licence that expired last month are not the same conversation, and a framework that raised both at one severity would make the second unfindable.
fields.label: Once Past Due
State-driven Severity
fields.description: v0.22.5. What a Date Field Role of State raises at. A state-driven rule has no band to be in and no expiry to be past, so none of the three band severities applies.

A JSON list of filters, ALL of which must hold for a row to be considered — `[{"field": "status", "op": "eq", "value": "Active", "default": "Active"}]`. Operators: eq, ne, gt, lt, gte, lte, in, nin, isnull, isnotnull, contains, ncontains. `default` is the value an EMPTY column is read as, which is how 'a policy with no status counts as Active' is said without a line of code — and getting it wrong is how a filter silently excludes every row that never had the field set. A filter naming a field this site has not got is skipped and reported in the sweep's warnings rather than refusing the whole rule. Empty list means every row of the target doctype.
fields.label: Scope Filters (JSON)

fields.description: A JSON object of NAMED INTERVALS a built-in scanner reads by name — {"spray_season_days": 120}. It exists because two of the shipped rules carry a second interval that `cadence_days` cannot hold: `water_test_stale` needs both the 90-day testing cadence and the 120-day spray season that gates it, and `audit_action_overdue` needs the grace period before a late action becomes a finding. Deliberately NOT a general-purpose configuration bag — every key in it is documented on the rule that reads it, and a key nothing reads is a setting somebody will one day change expecting something to happen.
fields.label: Extra Parameters (JSON)

fields.description: The one gate in this engine that is a question about OTHER ROWS. A finding stops being true when a LATER CLEAN RECORD FOR THE SAME SUBJECT supersedes it — a cabin re-inspected in September with nothing found says more about July's water stain than a checkbox does, and it requires nobody to remember a field. `{"subject_field": "unit", "clean_state_field": "workflow_state", "clean_state_values": ["Recorded"], "unreadable_counts_as_dirty": true}`. `doctype` and `date_field` default to the target's. `unreadable_counts_as_dirty` (the default) means a record whose state is empty or unreadable does NOT supersede: a result nobody can interpret is not evidence that anything is safe, and treating it as clean is how a compliance file becomes a clean record of nothing.
fields.label: Superseded By Later Clean (JSON)

fields.description: The alert's text, as a Jinja template rendered in a SANDBOX WITH NO FRAPPE IN IT — the row is available as `row` and by field name, plus `days_remaining`, `days_overdue`, `due_date`, `today`, `subject`, `regimes`, and the rule's own thresholds. The message is what somebody reads on a phone and decides on, so it should say what is true, what it costs, and what closes it. A message that only says 'expires soon' makes the reader open the record to learn anything, which is the work the alert existed to save.
fields.label: Message Template

fields.description: A field on the row carrying ITS OWN regime tags, copied onto each alert in place of the rule's — `regimes` on a training record, because the record says what that afternoon actually covered and the curriculum does not. An untagged row produces an untagged alert, deliberately: inventing a tag so the row is not bare would make the calendar claim coverage the register does not have.
fields.label: Per-row Regimes Field

fields.description: An ORDERED lookup that reads the regimes off a NAME rather than off a column, for the case `regimes_from_field` cannot reach — a certificate's audits come from its TYPE, and there is no tags column on it, only a name to read. First match wins and THE ORDER IS THE WHOLE CONTENT: `globalgap` must be checked before `gap`, because "GlobalGAP" contains "GAP" and a USDA GAP packet must not be handed another scheme's certificate. `[{"if_field_contains": {"field": ["cert_type", "cert_name"], "value": ["wps", "worker protection"]}, "then_regimes": ["WPS"]}, {"default_regimes": ["Internal"]}]`. Where entries name several fields, the FIELD ORDER IS THE OUTER LOOP: the whole table is tried against the type before any of it is tried against the name, so a word somebody typed on the day cannot retag a certificate whose type already said something. Overrides `regimes` per alert; the rule's own `regimes` stays the UNION of what this table can emit, which is what a one-regime sweep matches on.
fields.label: Regime Heuristics (JSON)

fields.description: The same ordered lookup, producing the alert's CATEGORY instead of its regimes — `[{"if_field_in": {"field": "cert_type", "value": ["Applicator License"]}, "then_category": "Workforce"}, {"default_category": "Certifications"}]`. One rule can fire on eleven kinds of certificate, and an applicator licence is a Workforce item while a GlobalGAP certificate is a Certifications one: the category is a property of the row, and a constant on the rule would file most of them under the wrong heading.
fields.label: Category Heuristics (JSON)
What it asks somebody to do

fields.description: The Farm Task Template this rule's work is done through. v0.41.0 REPOINTED THIS FIELD, and the reason is that it was aimed at the wrong size of thing: it used to name an Inspection Template, which is a MULTI-SECTION VISIT producing several compliance records from one trip, and a rule whose answer is 'test the smoke detector' has no sections. WHERE IT IS SET, THE TEMPLATE IS THE WHOLE RECIPE — the task type, the skill, the duration, the dispatch mode, the evidence contract, the record the completion produces and the checklist all come off it, and the `producer_farm_task_type`, `producer_skill_required` and `evidence_contract_json` fields beside it are not read at all. Those three stay as the FALLBACK for a rule with no template, which is most of them. Multi-section visits did not move and never depended on this field: the sweep bundles several overdue things at one place into one Inspection Session by matching the sections against the records the alerts ask for, deterministically, in _bundle_into_sessions.
fields.label: Producer Template

fields.description: The Farm Task type raised for this rule where no template is set — 'Inspection', 'Repair'. Same free-text vocabulary Farm Task.task_type uses, so the board filters without translation.
fields.label: Producer Task Type

fields.description: The crew skill the producer task needs — 'camp_maintenance', 'applicator'. Same vocabulary Farm Task.skill_required uses.
fields.label: Producer Skill
Producer Assignee Expression
fields.description: v0.22.5. A safe expression over the alert's source row producing an Employee — `row.foreman`. Where it is set, the producer task is assigned to that person directly and dispatch_mode is Dispatched; where it is empty, the task routes by skill as before. The two are exclusive: a task with a named holder is not in a pool.

What the producer task's completion must submit, as a JSON object using the same vocabulary an Inspection Template section does — `photos`, `signature`, `findings_text`, `witness`, `checklist_items`, `measurements`. A key outside it asks for nothing and looks like it asks for something, so it is refused here.
fields.label: Evidence Contract (JSON)

fields.description: The audits an alert from this rule is evidence for. Same vocabulary as every other regime tag in this app, picked rather than typed, so nobody writes OSHA where the vocabulary says OR-OSHA. A rule answering to no outside body carries `Internal` rather than nothing — an untagged alert is invisible to every regime filter, and silently invisible is the one thing a compliance calendar must not be.
fields.label: Regimes

fields.description: The regulations this rule enforces, with their citations — 'OAR 437-004-1120; 29 CFR 1910.142; FSMA Subpart L'. THE FIELD AN AUDITOR ASKS ABOUT, and the one that changes most often: when OR-OSHA renumbered heat illness from -1130 to -1131 this is the only thing that needed to move, and moving it is an edit rather than a release.
fields.label: Regulation Citations

fields.description: How long the records this rule watches must be kept, in years — 2 for WPS, 3 for OR-OSHA, 5 for NOP. 0 means the rule states no window of its own. It is carried on the rule because the retention obligation and the rule that produces the record come from the same paragraph of the same regulation.
fields.label: Retention (years)

fields.description: A JSON list of audit packet types whose readout includes this rule's alerts — ["FSMA", "OSHA"]. Validated against the packet types this app ships, because a packet name nobody generates is a claim that an alert reaches a document it never reaches. Empty means the alert is reachable by regime alone.
fields.label: Audit Packet Types (JSON)

fields.description: REQUIRED, AND IT IS PROSE. The sentence explaining what state makes this rule ripe rather than what date makes it due — and, just as importantly, what makes it stay quiet. A rule whose author cannot write that sentence has written a calendar reminder, which belongs in somebody's phone rather than in a compliance system. It is also the paragraph an auditor is read when they ask why an alert fired, so it should be true rather than aspirational.
fields.label: Kairotic Gate

fields.description: What goes wrong in the world when this condition is true and nobody acts — not what the paperwork looks like. It is what makes somebody read the alert rather than dismiss it.
fields.label: Purpose

fields.description: Who wrote this rule. `System` is one this app shipped; `Operator` is one somebody here authored; `AI-proposed` is one a model drafted from a regulation and A HUMAN HAS NOT NECESSARILY READ YET. The distinction is the whole audit story: at runtime every rule executes the same deterministic path, and the only thing that differs is who is answerable for the definition.
fields.label: Authored By

fields.description: Where an AI-proposed rule was read from — the URL and section of the regulation. It is what turns 'a model suggested this' into something a human can check, and a proposal without it is a claim with no source.
fields.label: AI Source Citation

fields.description: What about an AI-proposed rule needs a second pair of eyes, as a JSON list of flags written by `propose_compliance_rule` and never typed. `custom_python` means the model drafted a PROGRAM rather than a set of fields — the sandbox has already refused what it refuses, and this says a person still has to read what it left. `producer_assigned_to_expression` means the draft routes work to one named person. `supersedes_live_rule` means approving it will stand a running rule down. `approve_compliance_rule` refuses the code-shaped flags until the approver acknowledges them by name, which is the difference between reading a program and clicking past one.
fields.label: AI Review Flags

fields.description: The person who read this rule and accepted it. REQUIRED BEFORE `enabled` CAN BE SET — a rule that could fire without a name against it would make the calendar an assertion nobody signed, which is the exact failure the Configurable Compliance Framework exists to prevent.
fields.label: Approved By

fields.description: When they accepted it. Required alongside the approver, for the same reason a review date with nobody attached is one an auditor is trained to disbelieve.
fields.label: Approved On

fields.description: The approver as an Employee, where the site keeps a payroll register and the approval belongs to somebody on it. Optional: a rule approved by an administrator who is not an employee is still approved.
fields.label: Approver (Employee)

fields.description: The approver's signature, as a File. Optional, and it is the difference between a record of an approval and evidence of one — a scheme that asks for signed rule sets gets a signed rule set without anybody keeping a parallel binder.
fields.label: Approver Signature
Producer Inspection Template
fields.description: v0.207.0. The inspection the phone opens for this rule's work, when the work is an inspection rather than a task.

fields.label: Producer Wizard
fields.description: v0.207.0. A Wizard key (Farm Config Version) the phone opens for this rule's work.

fields.label: Loop Gap Accepted
fields.description: v0.207.0. Why this rule was enabled although audit_compliance_loop found a gap (accept_loop_gap on approve_compliance_rule).

name: Compliance Rule
